entry.title: China BOY: The "Great Ape" Who Turned Absurd Games into a Generation's Shared Language
entry.summary: China BOY, whose real name is Wang Hanzhe, is a Chinese gaming commentator, live streamer, and one of the most enduring figures in Bilibili's game section. Born on June 2, 1998, in Guiyang, Guizhou Province, he is known across the platform by his full handle,…
entry.content:
China BOY, whose real name is Wang Hanzhe, is a Chinese gaming commentator, live streamer, and one of the most enduring figures in Bilibili's game section. Born on June 2, 1998, in Guiyang, Guizhou Province, he is known across the platform by his full handle, China BOY Super Gorilla, a name that has become so synonymous with his persona that most viewers simply call him "China BOY" or "the Gorilla". His life story is one of unusual early independence and sustained self-direction. His mother passed away in December 2007, when he was nine years old, and he was subsequently raised by his grandmother. He began producing game commentary videos in 2012, at the age of fourteen, using little more than a mobile phone and a rudimentary understanding of video editing. After completing high school in 2016, he made the decision not to attend university, concluding that video creation offered a viable and meaningful career path. That same year, he moved alone from Guiyang to Shanghai to pursue content creation full-time, a decision that placed him among the earliest cohort of Chinese creators to treat online video as a profession rather than a hobby. As of late 2025, his Bilibili channel has over 10.5 million followers, and his total reach across Bilibili, Douyin, and other platforms exceeds twenty million.

China BOY's content is defined by a deliberate and consistent refusal to engage with the games that dominate mainstream gaming media. He rarely features competitive esports titles or AAA blockbusters. Instead, his videos are built around what Chinese internet culture calls "shadiao games," a term that translates roughly as absurdist, deliberately low-quality, or bizarrely conceived games that most creators would never consider covering. He has described himself as one of the people in China who has played the greatest number of these games, and the claim is credible. His library includes simulations of mundane occupations, horror games built almost entirely around jump scares, and independent titles that are technically crude but conceptually strange. His commentary transforms these games into comedic material through a combination of exaggerated reactions, absurdist commentary, and a voice that fans have described as one of the most distinctive in Chinese gaming content. The humor is not cruel; he treats even the worst games with a kind of affectionate curiosity, approaching them as artifacts of human creativity rather than as products to be evaluated. This stance distinguishes him from reviewers who approach games as consumers and from entertainers who treat bad games as targets for mockery. For China BOY, a strange game is an invitation to explore, and his willingness to take that invitation seriously is what makes his content compelling.

Among his most influential works is the "China BOY Commentary" series, which has been running in various forms since his earliest years on the platform. The series encompasses hundreds of videos across a wide range of games, and its longevity reflects the consistency of his creative voice. The 2013 series "Games Are Really Weird" established the template that he would refine over the following decade: a game that appears ordinary or poorly made is played with genuine curiosity, and the comedy emerges from the gap between the game's ambitions and its execution. The "Wang Xiansheng, Your Ghost Videos" series, in which he reacts to fan-made remixes and compilations of his own content, became one of his most popular recurring formats in the life section. His collaboration videos with other prominent Bilibili creators, particularly those in the loose collective sometimes referred to as the "Shanghai help group," including Lao Fanqie, Mou Huanjun, and Hu Shaobei, generated some of the platform's most-watched collaborative content. In 2022, he extended his creative reach into game development itself with the release of "A Piece of Poo" on Steam, a game in which players control a piece of excrement on a journey of self-improvement and combat, which accumulated hundreds of reviews and demonstrated his willingness to participate in the culture he had spent a decade commenting on.

China BOY's platform achievements are substantial and sustained. He has been selected for Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creator list in multiple years, including 2018, 2019, 2020, and 2023, a record of recognition that spans the platform's most formative period of growth. In 2018, he received Bilibili's Annual Danmaku Popularity Award, a recognition specifically tied to the interactive comment system that is central to the platform's culture. In 2019, he was named one of Tencent's Game Persons of the Year. His channel consistently ranks among the most-followed gaming accounts on Bilibili, and his average video performance reflects a loyal and engaged audience rather than a purely algorithmic one. Beyond Bilibili, he has maintained a significant presence on Douyin, where he is a signed game livestreamer, and he has been recognized as a contracted artist under Chao Dian Culture, one of the platform's major creator management agencies. In 2021, he participated in the "Long Scroll Treasure Hunt" project, a Bilibili initiative in which prominent creators introduced historical and cultural landmarks, and he served as the guardian of key revolutionary sites in the Yangtze River Delta region, including the First National Congress of the Communist Party of China Memorial.

The broader social significance of China BOY's career lies in his demonstration that sustained success in Chinese digital media does not require formal credentials, institutional backing, or conformity to the expectations of the gaming industry. He left school at eighteen and built a career through a combination of creative instinct, relentless output, and an intuitive understanding of what his audience found funny. His decision to focus on games that no one else would cover created a niche that he has occupied almost entirely on his own for over a decade. For young viewers who see their own interests as marginal or unserious, his work offers validation: the strange, the absurd, and the deliberately low-quality can be treated with the same attention and care that mainstream culture reserves for prestige objects. His movement from game commentary into life vlogs, music, writing, and game development reflects a creative restlessness that has allowed him to remain relevant as platform trends have shifted. In 2026, he published a book titled "Let It Rain, Make a Friend," extending his presence into yet another medium, and his recognition as a "Z-generation China BOY" by state media for his ability to "tell China's story with sincerity" suggests that his cultural influence has been acknowledged beyond the platform's own ecosystem.

In summary, China BOY represents a model of the creator as an intuitive cultural archivist of the absurd. He has spent more than a decade documenting the strangest corners of the gaming world, and in doing so he has built one of the most durable and recognizable personas on Bilibili. His career began with a fourteen-year-old filming himself playing games on a phone; it has since encompassed live streaming, music, writing, game development, and collaborations with some of the platform's most prominent figures. He has been selected for the Top 100 UP Creator list four times, received the platform's danmaku popularity award, and maintained a following of over ten million people through periods of significant change in Bilibili's content ecosystem. For Bilibili, he is a foundational figure in the game section, someone who helped define what gaming commentary could be in the platform's early years and who has continued to evolve alongside it. For viewers, he is a reminder that the most enduring creative work is often the least prestigious, and that a genuine interest in the strange and overlooked can be a foundation for a career that lasts.

entry.title: Fangstafu: The Paleontologist Couple Who Made Extinct Creatures Feel Alive
entry.summary: Fangstafu is a Chinese science communication channel operated by Tang Cheng and his wife Cai Chunlin, dedicated to paleontology, evolutionary biology, and the broader life sciences. The channel's name is a phonetic transliteration of the English phrase "fun stuff," reflecting its founders' conviction that scientific…
entry.content:
Fangstafu is a Chinese science communication channel operated by Tang Cheng and his wife Cai Chunlin, dedicated to paleontology, evolutionary biology, and the broader life sciences. The channel's name is a phonetic transliteration of the English phrase "fun stuff," reflecting its founders' conviction that scientific knowledge should be enjoyable, accessible, and emotionally resonant. Tang Cheng holds a doctorate from the Institute of Neuroscience at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, one of China's most prestigious research institutions, where his work focused on the neural mechanisms underlying animal behavior. Cai Chunlin, his wife and creative partner, manages the visual design, editing, and production aspects of the channel, creating the distinctive animated style that has become one of Fangstafu's most recognizable features. The couple began uploading videos to Bilibili in 2019, while Tang Cheng was still a doctoral student, and by 2020, after his graduation, they made the decision to pursue science communication as a full-time career rather than following the conventional academic path of postdoctoral research and university faculty positions. That decision, which Tang Cheng has described as a departure from what his academic training had prepared him for, has resulted in one of the most successful and critically respected science channels in China, with over 4.2 million followers on Bilibili as of early 2025 and a continuous presence on the platform's annual Top 100 UP Creator list since 2020.

The origin of Fangstafu's audience can be traced to a single video: "Anomalocaris: The Story of the First Hegemon," a thirty-minute animated documentary about a Cambrian-era predator that lived more than five hundred million years ago. The video, which combined rigorous paleontological research with a narrative structure that treated the ancient creature as a protagonist with a personality, ambitions, and a tragic destiny, accumulated millions of views and transformed the couple's hobby into a viable career. What made the video distinctive was not merely its subject matter, which had rarely been treated with such narrative seriousness in Chinese-language science communication, but its method. Tang Cheng approached the Anomalocaris not as a specimen to be described but as a character whose life could be reconstructed from fossil evidence. He explained the scientific debates surrounding the creature's anatomy, the competing hypotheses about its role in the Cambrian ecosystem, and the uncertainties that remain even after decades of research. The video did not simplify the science; it made the science feel urgent and dramatic by showing how paleontologists build knowledge from fragmentary evidence and how that knowledge changes as new fossils are discovered.

This commitment to narrative reconstruction has become Fangstafu's signature approach. The channel specializes in what its creators describe as "personified paleontology," a method in which extinct organisms are presented as characters whose behaviors, ecological roles, and evolutionary fates are explained through storytelling rather than through conventional lecture formats. The "Ghost Valley Chronicles" series, which focuses on the evolutionary history of vertebrates from fish to humans, represents the most ambitious expression of this approach. In one representative episode, the evolution of the mammalian ear is presented not as an anatomical transformation but as a story about the gradual repurposing of bones that once formed the jaw hinge of reptilian ancestors. The narrative follows the evidence: fossil intermediates, developmental biology, and comparative anatomy are woven together into a coherent account that respects scientific uncertainty while still providing a satisfying narrative arc. The series has been widely praised for its clarity and for its ability to make viewers feel that they are discovering the past alongside the researchers whose work is being described.

Beyond "Ghost Valley Chronicles," Fangstafu's content encompasses a wide range of topics within evolutionary biology and paleontology. The channel has produced episodes on the evolution of vision, the biology of parasites, the history of the domestication of plants and animals, and the ecological dynamics of mass extinction events. A recurring theme is the relationship between form and function: how the shape of a bone, the structure of an eye, or the arrangement of teeth can reveal what an organism ate, how it moved, and what pressures shaped its evolution. Tang Cheng's academic training in neuroscience informs his treatment of sensory biology, and several episodes have explored the evolution of the nervous system and the emergence of complex behavior. His wife Cai Chunlin's background in design and animation is evident in the visual style of the videos, which uses simple but expressive illustrations and animations to convey anatomical relationships and evolutionary sequences. The combination of scientific depth and visual clarity has made Fangstafu accessible to audiences ranging from university biology students to casual viewers with no formal scientific training.

The channel's institutional recognition has been substantial. Fangstafu received the Guokr Science Communication Contribution Award in 2020 and the Gezhi Science Communication Award as Creator of the Year in 2022. Tang Cheng was named one of Shanghai's "Science Stars" in 2025, a designation awarded by the municipal government to recognize outstanding contributions to public understanding of science. The channel has been selected for Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creator list in 2020, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025, a record of sustained recognition that places it among the platform's most consistently honored science accounts. In 2025, the "Ghost Valley Chronicles" series received the platform's Annual Original Program award, acknowledging the series' distinctive contribution to Bilibili's knowledge ecosystem. The couple has also collaborated with major brands and institutions, including a 2025 partnership with the mobile game Azur Lane for a public welfare initiative focused on mangrove conservation, which took them to Hainan Province to document wetland ecosystems.

The social value of Fangstafu's work lies in its demonstration that scientific rigor and popular accessibility are not competing objectives. Tang Cheng and Cai Chunlin have built a mass audience by treating their viewers as capable of understanding complex scientific ideas, provided those ideas are presented with sufficient clarity and narrative coherence. Their channel has filled a significant gap in Chinese-language science communication, which historically has been dominated by either technical academic content inaccessible to general audiences or superficial popularizations that sacrifice accuracy for entertainment. By occupying the space between these extremes, Fangstafu has helped establish a model for what serious science communication can look like on Chinese video platforms. For younger viewers, particularly those who may be considering careers in science, the channel offers a vision of scientific work as an ongoing process of discovery rather than a collection of settled facts. The couple's decision to leave conventional academic careers in order to pursue public communication full-time is itself a statement about the value they place on making science accessible, and their success suggests that this value is shared by millions of viewers.

In summary, Fangstafu represents a distinctive model of the creator as scientific storyteller. Tang Cheng and Cai Chunlin have combined advanced academic training with narrative skill and visual creativity to produce a body of work that is both scientifically rigorous and genuinely engaging. Their focus on paleontology and evolutionary biology, subjects that are often treated as remote and technical, has demonstrated that even the most ancient and unfamiliar forms of life can be made to feel immediate and meaningful when they are presented as characters in a story about survival, adaptation, and the long history of life on Earth. For Bilibili, Fangstafu is evidence that the platform's knowledge section can support creators who take intellectual risks and trust their audiences to follow. For the broader landscape of Chinese science communication, the channel is a reminder that the most effective educational content is often that which treats the audience not as passive recipients of information but as participants in the ongoing human project of understanding the natural world.

entry.title: Siwei Shiyanshi: The Self-Taught Polymath Who Turns Cold Knowledge into a Weapon of Curiosity
entry.summary: Siwei Shiyanshi, which translates as "Thinking Laboratory," is a Chinese knowledge creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's science and history section. His real name is Zhao Jiaqi, and he is based in Xi'an, Shaanxi Province. Before becoming a full-time content creator,…
entry.content:
Siwei Shiyanshi, which translates as "Thinking Laboratory," is a Chinese knowledge creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's science and history section. His real name is Zhao Jiaqi, and he is based in Xi'an, Shaanxi Province. Before becoming a full-time content creator, he worked as an ordinary office employee, a fact that distinguishes him from the many Bilibili knowledge creators who hold advanced degrees from elite universities. His parents were both middle school teachers, and he describes himself as a student whose strengths lay in the sciences while his humanities performance was unremarkable. He has never claimed academic credentials he does not possess, and this honesty about his background has become part of his appeal. His channel's official description is disarmingly modest: "Science and historical knowledge popularization, with thinking added in. This is Thinking Laboratory, created entirely at home by one person. Starting a business is hard, so please be patient with updates". That single sentence captures the essence of his practice: a solo creator working from his apartment, producing videos that combine scientific rigor, historical analysis, and philosophical reflection, all delivered with a sense of intellectual urgency that has attracted a devoted following.

Zhao Jiaqi began uploading to Bilibili around 2018, when the platform's knowledge section was still in its formative stages. His early videos were not polished productions; they were the work of a hobbyist experimenting with the tools available to him. What distinguished them from the outset was their intellectual range. He did not confine himself to a single discipline. His videos moved fluidly between biology, history, technology, physics, sociology, and anthropology, unified not by subject matter but by a method of inquiry that he has described as "thinking while popularizing". He approached every topic with the same question: what does this tell us about how the world actually works, and what can we learn from it about our own condition? This commitment to synthesis, to finding connections across seemingly unrelated domains of knowledge, became his signature. By 2022, his channel had grown to over 500,000 followers, and he began to be recognized as one of the most promising voices in Bilibili's knowledge ecosystem. By January 2025, his follower count had reached 7.275 million, and he was named to Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creator list for both 2023 and 2024, with a third selection following in 2026 for the 2025 list.

The most important turning point in Siwei Shiyanshi's career was his decision to produce a comprehensive series on the history of the Chinese Communist Party. This was not a subject he approached casually. He spent years researching, citing sources, and building a narrative that treats the Party's early history not as a triumphalist fable but as a case study in organizational survival, strategic adaptation, and the economic and social forces that shaped the outcome of the Chinese revolution. The series, which he began releasing as paid membership content on Bilibili's charging platform, became a phenomenon. It is widely credited with transforming his financial sustainability; discussions among his viewers note that "it was the Party history series that made him this successful," and that his paid membership numbers are among the highest in Bilibili's knowledge category, with over 180,000 users paying monthly for access to his content. The series covers topics ranging from the founding of the Party and the establishment of its first armed forces to the decision to embark on the Long March and the strategic choices that determined the outcome of the civil war. What makes the series distinctive is its analytical method: he approaches these events through the lenses of economics, organizational theory, and internal political dynamics rather than relying on ideological framing alone. One widely recommended episode, "How Did 'Not Taking a Single Needle or Thread from the Masses' Lead to Encircling the Cities from the Countryside?", uses economic reasoning to explain how the Red Army's relationship with rural populations became a strategic asset.

Beyond the Party history series, Siwei Shiyanshi's video library encompasses an extraordinary range of subjects. His videos on the history of pandemics, including the Black Death and the 1918 influenza outbreak, combine epidemiological analysis with social history. His science videos explore topics as varied as the biology of bacteria, the physics of spectroscopy, and the mechanics of nuclear disasters. His video on the Chernobyl disaster has been widely cited for its clear explanation of the reactor design flaws and the human decisions that compounded them. A characteristic work, "Why Do People Let Themselves Be Deceived? Lessons from Pacific Islanders," examines the psychology of deception through an anthropological lens, using a specific historical case to illuminate a universal human vulnerability. Another recurring theme in his work is the relationship between technology and social change: he has produced videos on space colonization, artificial intelligence, and the history of medical innovation, always asking not only how these developments work but what they mean for human society. His content is characterized by a density of information that rewards attentive viewing. He does not pad his videos with filler; every minute is spent building an argument or introducing evidence. His delivery is fast-paced, a characteristic that some viewers find demanding but that his loyal audience regards as a sign of respect for their time and intelligence.

The social value of Siwei Shiyanshi's work lies in his demonstration that serious intellectual content can thrive on a platform better known for entertainment. He has built a career not by simplifying complex ideas into easily digestible fragments but by trusting his audience to follow sustained, rigorous analysis. His Party history series, in particular, has reached an audience far beyond the typical viewership for academic history, and it has been used by students, professionals, and general viewers as a resource for understanding a period that is often taught in simplified terms. His willingness to engage with difficult and politically sensitive subjects through a lens of evidence and reasoning rather than dogma has earned him respect across a wide spectrum of viewers. At the same time, his work has not been without criticism. Some observers have questioned the depth of his sourcing, and he has been the subject of online controversy regarding his political positioning and the rigor of his historical claims. He has addressed these criticisms in his own videos, acknowledging the limitations of his research while defending the value of his approach. His response to controversy, characterized by a willingness to engage rather than retreat, reflects the intellectual honesty that his most committed viewers value most.

In summary, Siwei Shiyanshi represents a model of the creator as a self-taught public intellectual. He has no formal training in the subjects he covers, yet he has built one of the most substantial and financially successful knowledge channels on Bilibili by applying a consistent method of inquiry to an extraordinary range of topics. His Party history series, in particular, has demonstrated that there is a large audience for analytical, source-based history presented without condescension or oversimplification. For Bilibili, he is evidence that the platform's knowledge section can support creators who take intellectual risks and expect their audiences to follow. For viewers, he offers a reminder that curiosity is not the exclusive province of the credentialed, and that the most valuable education is often the one you give yourself. His long-term significance lies not in any single video or series but in the example he sets: that a person with a genuine desire to understand the world, and the discipline to pursue that understanding rigorously, can build something that matters.

entry.title: Bi Dao: The Tsinghua Chemist Who Turned Everyday Science into Comedy and Curiosity
entry.summary: Bi Dao, whose real name is Bi Xiaotian, is a Chinese science communicator, chemical engineering researcher, and one of the most recognizable educational creators on Bilibili. Born in the early 1990s, he completed his undergraduate and doctoral studies in chemical engineering at Tsinghua University, one…
entry.content:
Bi Dao, whose real name is Bi Xiaotian, is a Chinese science communicator, chemical engineering researcher, and one of the most recognizable educational creators on Bilibili. Born in the early 1990s, he completed his undergraduate and doctoral studies in chemical engineering at Tsinghua University, one of China's most prestigious institutions of higher education. His academic training was rigorous and conventional, focused on complex systems, mathematical modeling, and experimental research. Yet his public identity is anything but conventional. Under the name Bi Dao, which translates roughly as "Instructor Bi," he has built a following of more than five million users on Bilibili by applying serious scientific methods to absurdly ordinary questions: How can a person prevent splashing in a public toilet? Why do mosquitoes seem to target certain people more than others? What is the optimal strategy for eating hot pot without burning one's tongue? How can probability theory improve one's chances in a mobile game lottery? These questions may sound trivial, but the way Bi Dao answers them is anything but. He treats each one as a genuine research problem, complete with literature review, hypothesis formation, controlled experiments, mathematical modeling, and data analysis. The result is a body of work that has redefined what science communication can look like on Chinese video platforms.

Bi Dao began uploading videos to Bilibili around 2017, shortly after completing his doctorate. At the time, the platform's knowledge section was still emerging as a serious content category, and most educational creators either delivered traditional lecture-style lessons or produced short, shallow explainers designed for quick consumption. Bi Dao chose a different path. He combined the rigor of academic research with the pacing and humor of internet-native entertainment. His early videos were not polished productions; they were shot in his apartment, often featuring household objects arranged as makeshift laboratory equipment. But the substance was unmistakable. In his most famous early video, he investigated the physics of toilet splashing by building a scaled model, measuring the impact forces of falling objects on water surfaces, and deriving a formula that related splash height to the distance between the object and the water. The video was funny, but it was also correct. It demonstrated that a seemingly ridiculous question could be a legitimate entry point into fluid dynamics, mechanics, and experimental design.

What distinguishes Bi Dao from other science communicators on Bilibili is his commitment to the full scientific process rather than merely the presentation of conclusions. He does not simply tell viewers what scientists have discovered; he shows them what it looks like to be a scientist. His videos routinely include failed experiments, unexpected results, and moments when his initial hypothesis turns out to be wrong. He explains why he chose a particular experimental setup, what limitations it has, and how confident he is in the findings. This transparency is pedagogically valuable because it models intellectual honesty and teaches viewers that science is not a collection of facts but a method for asking questions and testing answers. His humor, which is dry, self-deprecating, and often absurd, serves as a delivery mechanism for this deeper lesson. He does not dumb down the science, but he makes it accessible by grounding it in experiences that every viewer has had.

Among his most representative works are videos on the physics of hot pot, the mathematics of mobile game gacha systems, the biology of mosquito attraction, and the engineering of everyday objects such as umbrellas and backpacks. His hot pot video, for example, used thermodynamic principles to explain why certain foods cook faster than others and how the shape of a pot affects heat distribution. His gacha video applied probability theory to calculate expected returns and demonstrated why players systematically overestimate their chances of winning rare items. These videos succeeded not because they provided practical advice, although they often did, but because they revealed the hidden mathematical and physical structures underlying ordinary experiences. Viewers who watched them came away with a sense that the world is more intelligible than it appears, and that scientific thinking is a tool available to anyone willing to ask questions.

Bi Dao's platform achievements are substantial. His Bilibili channel has accumulated over five million followers, and his videos have been viewed hundreds of millions of times. He has been featured in Bilibili's annual Top 100 UP Creator lists in multiple years, a recognition that places him among the platform's most influential knowledge creators. His content has been widely discussed on other social media platforms, including Weibo and Douyin, and he has collaborated with universities, science museums, and media organizations to promote public understanding of science. His academic credentials, including his doctorate from Tsinghua University, give him a level of authority that few science creators possess, but he wears that authority lightly. He never uses his credentials to shut down discussion or to claim that his conclusions are beyond question. Instead, he invites viewers to evaluate his methods and to think critically about the evidence he presents.

The broader social value of Bi Dao's work lies in his demonstration that science communication does not have to choose between rigor and entertainment. In China, as in many countries, there is a widespread assumption that serious scientific content cannot compete with entertainment content for young people's attention. Bi Dao's career disproves that assumption. He has built a mass audience by treating his viewers as intelligent adults who are capable of following complex reasoning and who appreciate being challenged rather than condescended to. His videos have contributed to a broader cultural shift in which scientific thinking is increasingly seen as a desirable attribute rather than a niche academic pursuit. For students who are considering careers in science and engineering, he offers a model of what a public intellectual can look like in the digital age: someone who is rigorous, humble, funny, and genuinely committed to helping others understand the world.

In summary, Bi Dao represents a distinctive model of the creator as public scientist. He has taken the skills he developed in a doctoral program, the curiosity that drives all good research, and the communication instincts of a natural teacher, and he has combined them into a body of work that is both entertaining and intellectually serious. His five million followers on Bilibili are not merely fans of comedy or fans of science; they are people who have discovered that learning can be enjoyable and that the most ordinary questions can lead to the most extraordinary insights. His long-term significance lies not in any single video or viral moment but in the example he sets: that a scientist can speak to the public without abandoning rigor, and that the public can embrace science without abandoning humor.

entry.title: Song Hao: The Mathematics Professor Who Became Bilibili's Most Trusted Teacher
entry.summary: Song Hao is a Chinese mathematics educator and one of the most influential academic content creators on Bilibili. Born in June 1979 in Wendeng, Shandong Province, he is an associate professor in the School of Statistics and Mathematics at Shandong University of Finance and Economics,…
entry.content:
Song Hao is a Chinese mathematics educator and one of the most influential academic content creators on Bilibili. Born in June 1979 in Wendeng, Shandong Province, he is an associate professor in the School of Statistics and Mathematics at Shandong University of Finance and Economics, where he also serves as director of the Quantitative Economics Teaching and Research Section and party branch secretary of the Practice Teaching Department in the School of Mathematics and Quantitative Economics. He completed his undergraduate and master's degrees in mathematics at Shandong University between 1997 and 2004, and later earned a doctorate from the Institute of Policy and Management at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2011. His entry into online video creation was not motivated by a desire for fame or commercial opportunity. In the early years of his teaching career, students repeatedly told him they could not follow his lectures or keep pace with the material. Rather than accept this as inevitable, Song Hao made a decision that would reshape his professional life: he began recording his complete lectures and uploading them online so that students could review them at their own pace, pause when they needed to think, and return to difficult concepts as many times as necessary. That decision, made with a second-hand camcorder and no expectation of an audience beyond his own classroom, set in motion one of the most remarkable educational projects in the history of Chinese digital media.

Song Hao's channel, officially named “Song Hao Teacher Official,” now has over 10.77 million followers on Bilibili and a total video view count exceeding 3.6 billion. His complete course on Advanced Mathematics, recorded in 154 lectures spanning 76 hours, has accumulated more than 150 million views and is frequently cited as the longest-watched video in Bilibili's history by total viewing time. His courses in Linear Algebra, Calculus, and Probability Theory and Mathematical Statistics consistently rank at the top of Bilibili's search results for their respective subjects, and his content is widely described as the default resource for Chinese university students seeking to pass or master compulsory mathematics courses. He has been named to Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list twice, first in 2023 and again in 2025, a recognition that places him among the platform's most respected knowledge creators.

What distinguishes Song Hao from the vast majority of educational creators on Chinese video platforms is his unwavering commitment to the classroom as the fundamental unit of instruction. His videos are not edited into short, punchy explainers or supplemented with flashy animations. They are complete, unedited recordings of his actual university lectures, delivered in real time, with a blackboard, chalk, and the same pacing he would use in front of a live audience. He insists on writing out every step of every derivation by hand, refusing to skip intermediate stages on the assumption that students can fill in the gaps themselves. This pedagogical philosophy is grounded in his observation that the students who struggle most with mathematics are not those who lack intelligence but those who have missed a single foundational step and then found themselves unable to recover. By recording the entire process, from the first line of a proof to the final numerical answer, he ensures that no student is left behind due to a gap in the recorded material.

His teaching style has been described as “breaking down complex problems into simple ones” and treating his viewers “as complete beginners,” a phrase that captures both his patience and his refusal to condescend. He has developed a set of mnemonic devices and memory aids that he calls the “Song-style seven-character formula” and the “onion method,” techniques designed to help students retain procedural knowledge without rote memorization. These devices are not gimmicks; they reflect a deep understanding of where students typically become confused and a deliberate effort to preempt those difficulties. He also incorporates everyday examples into his explanations, using analogies that make abstract mathematical concepts tangible without sacrificing rigor. His lectures are structured, methodical, and unhurried, and he has resisted pressure to shorten them or accelerate their pacing in response to trends in online content consumption.

The scale of Song Hao's impact on Chinese higher education is difficult to overstate. His Advanced Mathematics course alone has been viewed more than 150 million times, and his total video views across all courses exceed 3.6 billion. At a time when increasing numbers of Chinese students are entering universities and encountering mathematics courses that assume a level of preparation many do not possess, Song Hao's lectures have functioned as a de facto national tutoring service, available to anyone with an internet connection at no cost. His courses are particularly valuable for students at regional universities and vocational colleges who may not have access to the same quality of instruction as their peers at elite institutions. Media coverage of his work has repeatedly emphasized that his videos have “broken down the walls of the university campus,” making high-quality mathematics instruction available to learners regardless of their institutional affiliation or geographic location.

His institutional recognition reflects both his academic standing and his public impact. In addition to his two Top 100 UP Creator selections, he has received the first prize in the Ninth Shandong Provincial Teaching Achievement Awards and the second prize in the Eighth Shandong Provincial Teaching Achievement Awards. He has been named an Outstanding Communist Party Member in the Shandong Provincial Education System, a “Positive Energy Communication Ambassador” by Qilu Evening News, and one of Shandong University of Finance and Economics's “Most Beloved Teachers,” “Most Beautiful Teachers,” and “Top Ten Teachers.” These awards, typically reserved for classroom instructors with limited public profiles, take on additional significance when considered alongside his millions of online followers, suggesting that the academic establishment has recognized the legitimacy of his digital outreach rather than treating it as a distraction from his scholarly duties.

The broader social value of Song Hao's work lies in his demonstration that the most effective educational content is not necessarily the most innovative or entertaining. He has built an audience of over ten million people using nothing more than a camera, a blackboard, and a commitment to explaining every step of every problem. In an era when educational technology is often celebrated for its novelty, his success is a reminder that the fundamentals of good teaching, patience, clarity, and genuine concern for the student's understanding, remain unchanged. His lectures have been watched by students preparing for graduate entrance examinations, by working professionals seeking to refresh their mathematical skills, and by curious learners who simply want to understand a subject they found intimidating in school. His willingness to make his teaching freely available, without paywalls or subscription fees, reflects a conviction that knowledge should not be treated as a commodity to be sold but as a public good to be shared.

In summary, Song Hao represents a model of the educator as public servant, someone who has used the tools of digital media to extend the reach of the classroom far beyond its physical walls. His decision to record his lectures was pragmatic, driven by the needs of a handful of students who were struggling, but its consequences have been transformative for millions. He has been recognized by Bilibili as one of its Top 100 creators, by provincial education authorities as an exemplary teacher, and by his students and viewers as a trusted guide through one of the most intimidating subjects in the university curriculum. His long-term significance lies not in any single video or series but in the principle he has demonstrated: that the most valuable educational content is often the least flashy, and that a teacher who is genuinely committed to the success of every student, even those he will never meet, can build something that lasts.

entry.title: Peng Zhihui (ZhiHuiJun): The "Wild Iron Man" Who Built Robots in His Bedroom and Then Built a Company
entry.summary: Peng Zhihui, known across Chinese digital platforms by his online handle ZhiHuiJun, which translates roughly as "The Young Hui Gentleman," is one of the most unusual figures in Bilibili's history. He is simultaneously a creator with over 2.8 million followers, a former member of Huawei's…
entry.content:
Peng Zhihui, known across Chinese digital platforms by his online handle ZhiHuiJun, which translates roughly as "The Young Hui Gentleman," is one of the most unusual figures in Bilibili's history. He is simultaneously a creator with over 2.8 million followers, a former member of Huawei's elite "Genius Youth" program, and the co-founder, president, and chief technology officer of AgiBot, a robotics company valued in the billions. His story is not merely one of online fame but of a career trajectory that moved from bedroom tinkering to industrial-scale innovation without ever losing the creative curiosity that first attracted an audience. Born in 1993 in Ji'an, Jiangxi Province, Peng graduated from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) with a bachelor's degree from the School of Life Science and Technology in 2015 and a master's degree from the School of Information and Communication Engineering in 2018.He then worked as an algorithm engineer at OPPO's AI Lab before joining Huawei's "Genius Youth" program in 2020, where he worked on Ascend AI chips and AI algorithms.In 2023, he left Huawei and co-founded AgiBot with his UESTC alumnus Deng Taihua, serving as the company's president and CTO.Throughout this entire period, he continued to upload videos to Bilibili under the name ZhiHuiJun, documenting his personal engineering projects with a level of technical depth and production quality that has made him a singular figure in China's maker community.

What sets ZhiHuiJun apart from virtually every other technology creator on Bilibili is the sheer ambition of the projects he undertakes as a solo creator. He does not review products or explain concepts from a distance; he builds things that most people would assume require a team of engineers and a well-funded laboratory. His breakout project, released in October 2021, was a small, high-precision six-axis robotic arm that he designed, built, programmed, and filmed entirely on his own. The arm, which he named Dummy, was capable of performing tasks as delicate as threading a needle through a grape's skin, and the video documenting its construction and operation accumulated millions of views and became one of the most discussed technology videos of the year in China.The project demonstrated not only his technical range, spanning mechanical design, industrial modeling, motor selection, control programming, and AI vision, but also his ability to communicate that complexity in a way that was engaging rather than intimidating. He followed Dummy with a series of equally ambitious projects: an autonomous bicycle that could balance itself and navigate without a rider, a miniaturized Linux computer the size of a coin, a modular mechanical keyboard, and a Mars rover constructed from crab shells.Each project was documented in a video that combined technical explanation, behind-the-scenes documentation of failures and iterations, and a narrative arc that made the final result feel earned rather than inevitable.

The stylistic signature of ZhiHuiJun's content is a combination of understated delivery and extraordinary technical substance. He does not rely on exaggerated reactions or dramatic editing; his voice is calm and matter-of-fact, and his videos often run fifteen to thirty minutes, a length that requires genuine viewer investment. What makes them compelling is the visible evidence of problem-solving. He shows the moments when a design fails, when a component does not work as expected, when he has to rethink an approach. This willingness to document the messy reality of engineering, rather than presenting only the polished final product, distinguishes him from creators who treat technology as a spectacle to be consumed rather than a practice to be understood. His audience, which includes both professional engineers and curious laypeople, responds to this authenticity. The nickname "Wild Iron Man" that fans gave him captures both the ambition of his projects and the do-it-yourself ethos that defines his creative identity.

ZhiHuiJun's platform achievements are substantial, though his follower count is smaller than that of some of Bilibili's most popular entertainment creators. As of January 2026, his Bilibili account has approximately 2.84 million followers, and his Weibo account has over one million.He was named a Bilibili Top 100 UP Creator for 2021, and his videos routinely accumulate millions of views. His influence, however, is not measured solely by platform metrics. In 2024, he was named to the Hurun China U30 list of young entrepreneurs and to Fortune China's 40 Under 40 list of business elites.In 2025, he was selected as one of the year's AI Figures, sharing the stage with Wang Xingxing, the founder of Unitree Robotics, a recognition that placed him among the most significant figures in China's embodied AI sector.His company, AgiBot, has become one of the leading players in China's humanoid robotics industry, and its 2025 acquisition of a controlling stake in the publicly listed Shangwei New Materials, valued at approximately 550 billion yuan, made him the chairman of a major A-share listed company at the age of thirty-two.

The broader significance of ZhiHuiJun's career lies in his demonstration that individual technical creativity and large-scale industrial ambition are not mutually exclusive. He began as a self-taught maker who used the Bilibili platform to share projects that no one had asked him to build, and he has ended up leading a company that is competing at the frontier of global robotics. His videos are not promotional content for his company; they are the record of a personal practice that predates and transcends his commercial success. For aspiring engineers and makers, he offers a model of how to develop deep technical skills through self-directed projects, how to communicate those skills to a broad audience without simplifying them into triviality, and how to transition from individual creativity to organizational leadership without abandoning the curiosity that started it all. His advice to students at his alma mater in 2026, that "good questions are becoming more precious than answers" and that "knowledge only becomes judgment after it is tested by practice," encapsulates a philosophy that is visible in everything he has built.

In summary, Peng Zhihui represents a distinctive model of the creator as engineer-entrepreneur, someone who built an audience by doing genuinely difficult things in public and then built an institution to do them at scale. His Bilibili channel is not merely a portfolio but a living archive of intellectual and practical development, from a coin-sized computer to a robotic arm capable of surgery-adjacent precision to the founding of a company that is now valued in the tens of billions. For Bilibili, he is evidence that the platform's technology section can nurture creators whose work has consequences far beyond the screen. For the broader landscape of Chinese innovation, he is a reminder that the most transformative careers often begin not with a business plan but with a camera, a workbench, and a stubborn refusal to accept that something is impossible.

entry.title: Zhiliaojieya Mengwu: The One-Man Studio Bringing the World's Most Overlooked Animals to Millions
entry.summary: Zhiliaojieya Mengwu, whose real name is Peng Xianbo, is a Chinese wildlife content creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's knowledge section. Operating as a completely independent one-man studio, he has built an audience of over 4.3 million followers on Bilibili as…
entry.content:
Zhiliaojieya Mengwu, whose real name is Peng Xianbo, is a Chinese wildlife content creator and one of the most distinctive voices in Bilibili's knowledge section. Operating as a completely independent one-man studio, he has built an audience of over 4.3 million followers on Bilibili as of January 2025, with his content focused on the natural stories of rare, unconventional, and frequently misunderstood animals. His channel name, which translates roughly to "Got It, Stress-Relief Cute Creatures," is deliberately playful, but the work itself is anything but frivolous. Peng has been selected for Bilibili's annual Top 100 UP Creators list for three consecutive years, from 2022 through 2024, and in 2025 he received the platform's "Annual Public Welfare UP Creator" award, a recognition that reflects the social mission embedded in his work. His videos have been described as a "stress-relief zone for graduate school entrance exam preparation" and "the Animal World for a new generation," a formulation that captures both their calming effect and their role as an accessible entry point into natural history.

Peng Xianbo's path to becoming one of Bilibili's most recognized wildlife communicators was neither planned nor straightforward. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he found himself with time on his hands and turned to video creation as a way to make a living. His initial forays into the platform were in the guichu or "ghost畜" genre, a style of remix video that was popular on Bilibili at the time but which had begun to decline in both viewership and monetization potential. Recognizing that the format was no longer sustainable, he made a strategic pivot based on his academic background: he had studied animal medicine in university, and he decided to apply that training to a new creative direction. The transition was not immediate or easy. In the early period, his monthly income was only one or two thousand yuan, insufficient to cover his basic expenses, and each video required five to six days of production, with scripts exceeding two thousand words and AI voiceover meticulously adjusted for quality. He has since described those first two years as a period of "stubbornly grinding it out," during which he could barely afford rent and had to rely on sheer persistence to continue.

What distinguishes Zhiliaojieya Mengwu from the vast field of animal content on Chinese video platforms is his deliberate focus on species that most creators overlook. Rather than featuring domestic pets or the charismatic megafauna that dominate traditional wildlife programming, he specializes in snakes, insects, and other creatures that are typically regarded with fear, disgust, or indifference. His videos present these animals through a documentary-style approach, combining carefully sourced footage with humorous and accessible narration that reframes them as fascinating rather than threatening. He describes his own work as "non-serious science communication," a phrase that signals both his rejection of academic solemnity and his commitment to accuracy. His content operates on two distinct tracks: one track uses curated internet footage to create light, entertaining science videos that introduce viewers to animal behaviors and biological facts, while the other track involves original field documentation, often produced in collaboration with conservation organizations such as the SEE Foundation, to record wildlife in China's nature reserves and national parks. The latter track has taken him to locations such as the Chongzuo Nature Reserve in Guangxi, where he documented the white-headed langur and other protected species as part of a public welfare initiative with the mobile game Azur Lane. The structural variety of his output allows him to serve audiences with different levels of engagement, from casual viewers seeking entertainment to those genuinely interested in conservation and biodiversity.

Among his most representative works are videos such as "The Jaguar: What Era Are We Living In," "Failure Means Becoming a Box: The Courtship Stories of Unpopular Animals," and "Animal World's Version of Three Heroes Fighting Lu Bu: A Pride of Lions Takes On a Nile Crocodile". These titles exemplify his distinctive approach to naming and framing: they draw on internet slang, classical literary references, and absurdist humor to make the subject matter immediately engaging, while the content itself remains grounded in accurate biological information. His video about the Tibetan fox, titled "As Long As the Green Hills Remain," uses the animal's distinctive facial expression, which has become a meme in Chinese internet culture, as a hook to discuss its habitat, behavior, and conservation status. Another characteristic work, "The Clouded Leopard: Living Fossils of the Forest," combines footage of the rarely seen predator with narration that explains its evolutionary history and the threats it faces. His field documentation in Guangxi, produced with the SEE Foundation and featuring voice actor Ge Ping as an "animal observer," represents his most ambitious production to date, blending original footage with conservation messaging and a narrative structure that positions viewers as witnesses to the work of protecting endangered species.

The platform achievements of Zhiliaojieya Mengwu are substantial and reflect the growing appetite for science content on Bilibili. In June 2022, his rare animal science videos reached the top of Bilibili's "dark horse" growth chart, with his account gaining 1.148 million followers in a single quarter and a single-day peak of 57,700 new followers. At that time, his total follower count was only around 200,000, meaning that his growth during that period represented a more than fivefold increase. By January 2025, his follower count had reached 4.331 million, and his content has continued to accumulate millions of views across his video library. His three consecutive years on the Top 100 UP Creators list, from 2022 through 2024, place him among a select group of knowledge creators who have achieved sustained recognition, and his 2025 "Annual Public Welfare UP Creator" award specifically acknowledged the conservation dimension of his work. His selection alongside creators such as Luo Xiang, Lao Fanqie, Muyu Shuixin, and MediaStorm on the 2024 Top 100 list underscores his position within the platform's most influential cohort.

The broader social value of Peng Xianbo's work lies in his demonstration that conservation communication can be genuinely popular without resorting to either alarmism or sentimentality. By focusing on species that are typically ignored or feared, he expands his audience's understanding of biodiversity beyond the narrow range of animals that receive mainstream attention. His collaboration with conservation organizations and his participation in public welfare initiatives, including the "E Qi Shou Hu Di Qiu" environmental short video program organized by the SEE Foundation, position him as a bridge between digital content creation and on-the-ground conservation efforts. For viewers who may never encounter these animals in person, his videos offer a form of vicarious natural history education that is both entertaining and ethically grounded. His insistence on operating as a one-man studio, handling scripting, production, and business negotiations himself, also represents a distinctive model of independent creative practice that stands apart from the team-based structures of many comparable channels.

In summary, Zhiliaojieya Mengwu is a creator whose significance lies in his ability to find wonder in the overlooked corners of the natural world. He has built a successful career not by chasing trends or adopting the formats of his competitors, but by applying his academic training and personal curiosity to subjects that others have neglected. His three consecutive years on Bilibili's Top 100 list, his 4.3 million followers, and his 2025 public welfare award are all evidence that this approach has resonated with a large and loyal audience. For Bilibili, he represents the knowledge section at its most accessible and its most purposeful. For viewers, he offers a reminder that the most rewarding discoveries are often found in places we have been taught not to look. And for the broader landscape of Chinese digital culture, his career is a testament to the possibility of building a sustainable creative practice on the foundations of patience, expertise, and a genuine commitment to sharing the world's strangest and most wonderful creatures with anyone willing to pay attention.

entry.title: Muyu Shuixin: The Filmmaker Who Turned Long-Form Film Analysis into a National Classroom
entry.summary: Muyu Shuixin is a Chinese film and television commentator who has quietly become one of the most influential creators in Bilibili's history. Unlike many of his peers, he has never relied on viral gimmicks, shocking challenges, or personality-driven spectacle. Instead, he has built a career…
entry.content:
Muyu Shuixin is a Chinese film and television commentator who has quietly become one of the most influential creators in Bilibili's history. Unlike many of his peers, he has never relied on viral gimmicks, shocking challenges, or personality-driven spectacle. Instead, he has built a career on the patient, rigorous, and deeply literary analysis of films, television series, and animated works. His channel, which he began in August 2013 with an animation tutorial titled "Muyu Animation Classroom Episode 1: Insert Shots (FLCL)," has evolved over more than a decade into a cornerstone of Bilibili's film and television section, accumulating over 14 million followers and a reputation for intellectual seriousness that few creators on the platform can match. As of early 2025, his Bilibili account reported 14.05 million followers, and by late 2026 that number had grown to approximately 14.6 million, placing him among the platform's most-followed individual creators. His selection to Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list for eight consecutive years, from 2018 through 2025, is a distinction shared by only a handful of figures, and it reflects a sustained commitment to quality that has outlasted multiple cycles of platform trends.

Muyu Shuixin's personal background is deliberately obscure. He has never publicly disclosed his real name, his educational history, or the details of his early life, and he maintained a strict policy of not appearing on camera for the first decade of his career. When he finally revealed his face in a March 2024 video titled "After 10 Years as a Creator, an Introvert Finally Decides to Appear," he wore a mask, preserving the anonymity that had become a defining feature of his public persona. His channel name is derived from a classical Chinese idiom, "climbing a tree to seek fish and using clear water to mirror the heart" (缘木求鱼，白水鉴心), a phrase that suggests both the futility of certain pursuits and the value of self-reflection. This refusal to trade on personal biography is not merely a quirk; it is a deliberate artistic choice that directs the viewer's attention entirely to the work itself, to the films being analyzed and the ideas being explored. In an era when creator personality is often the primary product, Muyu Shuixin has built his audience on the strength of his analysis alone.

What distinguishes Muyu Shuixin's content from the vast field of Chinese film commentary is its extraordinary depth and its literary quality. His videos typically run between thirty and sixty minutes, and many of his most ambitious projects exceed that range significantly. His commentary is characterized by what Chinese media scholars have described as a multi-layered interpretive framework that includes close textual reading, artistic analysis, theoretical self-awareness, and real-world engagement. He does not merely summarize plots or offer superficial opinions; he situates each work within its historical context, compares different adaptations and source materials, and draws connections to broader cultural and philosophical questions. His voice, which has been described as magnetic and reminiscent of a late-night radio host, is a central element of his appeal, but it is the substance of his scripts that has earned him the loyalty of an audience that is willing to invest hours in a single video. He has been likened to a "video version of Dangnian Mingyue," a reference to the popular historian whose accessible yet rigorous writing brought the Ming dynasty to millions of readers, and the comparison captures the way his work functions as public education rather than mere entertainment.

His most celebrated achievement is arguably his fifty-episode, forty-five-minute-per-episode complete analysis of *Water Margin* (水浒传), one of China's four great classical novels. The series, which he began in late 2021, was not a simple retelling of the story but a comprehensive examination that incorporated multiple television adaptations, the original novel, related classical texts such as *The Thirty-Six Heroes of Song Jiang* and *The宣和遗事*, and folk theatrical traditions. Fans have compared his narration to the legendary storytelling of Shan Tianfang, a master of Chinese oral performance, and the series has been described as a "treasure of the platform" for its exhaustive research and clear presentation. Other major projects include his full analysis of *Dream of the Red Chamber*, his series on *The Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, his deep dive into *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*), and his interpretations of contemporary works such as *The Awakening Age* and *The Bad Kids*. His analysis of *The Bad Kids*, a drama about the moral complexity of juvenile crime, drew thousands of comments from viewers engaging with questions of narrative logic, cinematography, and social responsibility.

The commercial realities of Muyu Shuixin's career reveal the paradoxes of Bilibili's creator economy. In April 2023, he published a public statement acknowledging that he had not received a single advertising commission in over four months and that Bilibili's creator incentive payments were insufficient to cover his office rent. The disclosure, which came amid a broader debate about a "wave of creators stopping updates" on the platform, attracted widespread media attention and prompted reflection on the sustainability of long-form, high-cost content production. He described his work as "creating for love," a phrase that captured both his commitment to quality and his frustration with an economic model that struggled to support it. In 2024, he launched a paid membership program called "Starry Sky Reading Club," in which he appeared on camera for the first time (still wearing a mask), and he continued to update his *Shiji* series, demonstrating that his audience was willing to support his work directly. His ability to survive a period of financial precarity without compromising his creative standards is a testament to the loyalty he has cultivated and the perceived value of his output.

The social and cultural significance of Muyu Shuixin's work extends beyond the platform metrics. He has been credited with helping to legitimize long-form video analysis as a serious intellectual genre in China, demonstrating that viewers will commit hours of attention to content that treats them as capable of engaging with complex ideas. His videos on classical literature have functioned as a form of adult education, introducing millions of viewers to texts they might never have approached in written form. His decision to analyze *Water Margin* with reference to multiple adaptations and historical sources has been praised for encouraging viewers to think critically about the relationship between source material and adaptation, between historical context and contemporary interpretation. At a time when Chinese digital culture is often criticized for prioritizing speed and sensation over depth, Muyu Shuixin represents a counterexample: a creator who has built a massive audience by doing the opposite of what the algorithms supposedly reward.

In summary, Muyu Shuixin is a creator whose significance lies not in his personality but in his practice. He has demonstrated that anonymity, patience, and intellectual rigor can be viable foundations for a career in digital media, and that an audience exists for content that respects their time and their intelligence. His eight consecutive years on Bilibili's Top 100 list, his fourteen million followers, and his enduring influence on the platform's film and television section are all evidence of this. For Bilibili, he is a symbol of what the platform aspires to be when it takes its knowledge mission seriously. For viewers, he is a teacher in the truest sense, someone who does not merely explain what a film means but teaches how to watch, how to read, and how to think. And for the broader landscape of Chinese online culture, his career is a reminder that the most durable creative work is often the least performative, built not on the cult of personality but on the quiet accumulation of insight and craft.

entry.title: Xiao Yuehan Kehan: The Historian Who Built a Universe Out of Tongliao and Taught Millions to See the World from Below
entry.summary: Xiao Yuehan Kehan, whose real name is simply Xiao Yuehan, is a Chinese history content creator and one of the most influential figures in Bilibili's knowledge section. He is a native of Tongliao, a city in Inner Mongolia, and he operates his channel as a…
entry.content:
Xiao Yuehan Kehan, whose real name is simply Xiao Yuehan, is a Chinese history content creator and one of the most influential figures in Bilibili's knowledge section. He is a native of Tongliao, a city in Inner Mongolia, and he operates his channel as a solo creator, a fact that is all the more remarkable given the scale of his reach. As of March 2026, his Bilibili channel has over 10.62 million followers, making him the first creator in Bilibili's knowledge category to surpass the ten-million mark. Before becoming a video creator, he was an active answerer on Zhihu, the Chinese question-and-answer platform, where he wrote extensively on Soviet history, military affairs, and international politics under the name "Little John," a reference to the operational codename of Frank Underwood in the American television series *House of Cards*. His Zhihu answers accumulated a substantial following, and when he began uploading videos to Bilibili in November 2020, his early content consisted largely of curated selections from those written answers. His breakthrough was immediate: his first major video, "Why Was the Soviet Union So Powerful?", released on November 14, 2020, has accumulated over 33.9 million views as of August 2025, a figure that remains one of the highest in Bilibili's knowledge category.

What distinguishes Xiao Yuehan Kehan from the crowded field of Chinese history educators is his construction of an entire narrative and linguistic universe around a set of recurring themes and a highly distinctive lexicon. He organizes his content into several ongoing series. The "Bizarre Small Nations" series examines the histories of countries that are largely absent from mainstream historical discourse: The Gambia, Nauru, Burkina Faso, Albania, and dozens of others, each treated with the same seriousness and narrative care that larger nations typically receive. The "Hardcore Ruthless People" series abandons the traditional focus on kings, generals, and statesmen, instead telling the stories of criminals, con artists, spies, soldiers, and ordinary people whose lives intersected with the great upheavals of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in unexpected ways. The "Bizarre Organizations" series applies the same approach to institutions, from intelligence agencies to revolutionary cells. And the "Little John" series operates as a kind of adult fairy tale, using the conventions of fantasy narrative to pose questions about human psychology and historical development. Across all these series, he maintains a commitment to what Chinese critics have described as a "people's history" perspective, a historiographical approach that prioritizes the experiences of ordinary individuals over the actions of elites and that seeks to understand historical events through the material conditions and social forces that shaped them.

The linguistic dimension of Xiao Yuehan Kehan's work is arguably as important as its historical content. He has developed a distinctive vocabulary and set of running jokes that his fans refer to collectively as the "Tongliao Universe" (通辽宇宙). The most famous of these is his use of Tongliao itself as a unit of measurement: when describing the area of a foreign country, he will often compare it to his hometown, producing statements such as "Albania is only half a Tongliao." This running gag has become so iconic that "Tongliao" (abbreviated as "T") now functions as a semi-serious unit of area measurement within his community, and the phrase "nT" is used by fans to express the size of any territory. He employs puns, dialect expressions, and colloquial idioms drawn from northeastern Chinese speech, and he has a talent for coining memorable nicknames for historical figures, such as "Soviet Cousin" for Leonid Brezhnev and "American Cousin" for Richard Nixon, that have entered the broader vocabulary of Chinese internet culture. This linguistic creativity has spawned a wave of imitation among other history creators and has been credited with fundamentally altering the style of Chinese online history communication, making it more playful, more accessible, and more attentive to the rhetorical strategies that sustain audience engagement.

The commercial and institutional recognition of Xiao Yuehan Kehan's work has been substantial and consistent. He was named to Bilibili's Top 100 UP Creators list for four consecutive years, from 2021 through 2024, and in 2022 he received the platform's "Highest Popularity" award in addition to his Top 100 designation. In January 2026, he was again recognized as one of the 2025 Top 100 UP Creators. His average video receives over three million views, and his collaboration with Xinhua News Agency in December 2021, a "Hardcore Ruthless People" episode about the British spy George Blake, was widely praised as a model for how independent creators could engage with mainstream institutions without sacrificing their distinctive voice. A commentator at the time observed that the episode demonstrated that "telling China's story does not necessarily require telling a Chinese story," a formulation that captures the universalist ambition underlying his work. In 2023, he co-authored a book titled *Heroes and the Times* with two other history writers, extending his reach from video into print media.

The broader social significance of Xiao Yuehan Kehan's project lies in his demonstration that historical knowledge can be both intellectually rigorous and genuinely popular without compromising either quality. He cites sources and includes reference lists in his videos, yet he presents his material with the pacing and narrative momentum of a serialized drama. His choice of subjects, small nations and obscure individuals rather than great powers and famous leaders, reflects a deliberate political and ethical commitment to expanding his audience's understanding of the world beyond the narrow frame that mainstream media typically provides. For young Chinese viewers, many of whom have limited exposure to the histories of the Global South or to the lived experiences of ordinary people in distant places, his videos offer an education that is both geographically and socially broadening. At the same time, his work has not been without controversy; in 2025, a video in his "Hardcore Ruthless People" series was found to contain serious factual errors, prompting him to issue a public apology and acknowledge that his content production relied on a single external researcher whose sourcing had proven unreliable. His handling of the incident, including a self-deprecating reference to "poor quality control" in a subsequent video, was received by many fans as a genuine acknowledgment of fallibility rather than a defensive deflection, and it arguably strengthened rather than damaged his credibility by demonstrating that he takes his audience's trust seriously.

In summary, Xiao Yuehan Kehan represents a distinctive model of the creator as a public historian, one who treats the video platform as a space for serious intellectual work while refusing to abandon the entertainment value that makes that work accessible to a mass audience. His Tongliao Universe is not merely a collection of running jokes but a coherent rhetorical system that binds together his diverse subject matter and creates a sense of shared community among his viewers. His commitment to a people's history perspective gives his work an ethical orientation that distinguishes it from both conventional academic history and the personality-driven content that dominates much of the platform. And his willingness to acknowledge error and to continue producing work in the face of criticism suggests a maturity that is rare in the often volatile ecosystem of online knowledge production. For Bilibili, he is a cornerstone of the platform's knowledge section and a demonstration that independent creators can achieve both popularity and intellectual seriousness. For viewers around the world, he offers a model of historical storytelling that is rooted in a specific place, Tongliao, but speaks to a universal curiosity about how ordinary people have lived, struggled, and survived in a world shaped by forces far larger than themselves.

entry.title: MediaStorm and Tim Pan: How a Self-Taught Filmmaker Built China's Most Ambitious Video Production Studio on Bilibili
entry.summary: MediaStorm, known in Chinese as Yingshi Jufeng, is a Chinese filmmaking and technology content studio founded and operated by Pan Tianhong, who is universally known by his English name, Tim. Born in 1996 in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, Tim is a graduate of the University of…
entry.content:
MediaStorm, known in Chinese as Yingshi Jufeng, is a Chinese filmmaking and technology content studio founded and operated by Pan Tianhong, who is universally known by his English name, Tim. Born in 1996 in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, Tim is a graduate of the University of Kent in the United Kingdom, where he studied film. His path to becoming one of Bilibili's most recognized creators was neither linear nor conventional. By his own account and according to media profiles, he was a self-described "internet-addicted teenager" and a poor student during his early years, a young person whose parents and teachers had little reason to expect academic distinction. He left China after middle school to study abroad, eventually earning a degree in film. In 2014, while still a student, he created the MediaStorm account, and in 2015 he uploaded his first video to the internet. After returning to China in 2017, he assembled a small studio team and began producing content focused on filmmaking equipment reviews, technical tutorials, and original short films. What began as a one-person operation has since grown into a company with over 150 employees, annual revenue exceeding one hundred million yuan, and a multi-platform audience exceeding forty million followers, with more than seventeen million on Bilibili alone as of September 2026.

MediaStorm's creative identity is defined by an unusual combination of technical rigor and cinematic ambition. The studio's primary output falls into several overlapping categories: meticulous reviews of cameras, lenses, and production equipment; instructional content that teaches viewers the practical skills of filmmaking, from lighting and composition to editing and color grading; and original short films and documentary projects that demonstrate the techniques being taught. This tripartite structure, in which the studio both explains how filmmaking works and then produces work that exemplifies those principles, distinguishes MediaStorm from creators who specialize in only one mode. The production values of the channel are consistently exceptional; MediaStorm has been described by viewers and critics as "Bilibili's standard-bearer for image quality," a reputation earned through a commitment to shooting in high resolution, employing professional-grade equipment, and investing heavily in post-production. Tim's on-camera presence is similarly distinctive: he is articulate, technically fluent, and visibly enthusiastic about the craft of filmmaking, but he avoids the performative personality-driven style that characterizes many of Bilibili's most popular creators. His videos feel less like entertainment and more like an invitation into a professional workshop, where the viewer is treated as a serious participant rather than a passive spectator.

Among MediaStorm's most significant works is the 2020 documentary "Ascent: We Flew to 30,000 Meters Together," a project that involved launching a high-altitude balloon carrying professional cameras to capture 8K, 360-degree panoramic footage of the Earth's curvature and the near-space environment.
